provenance.note: Abdominal wall and inguinal canal (Anatomy 2, 2024-25) (Anatomy 2, Pr. A. Majbar)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Rule of 3: skin, Camper's, Scarpa's / EO, IO, TA / transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum.
EO lower edge = inguinal ligament; aponeurosis = superficial ring.
IO gives cremaster; IO + TA = conjoint tendon.
Rectus sheath; linea alba; arcuate line: no posterior sheath below.
Umbilical remnants: round ligament, median and medial umbilical ligaments.
Lymph above umbilicus → axillary; below → superficial inguinal.
Weak areas: umbilicus, linea semilunaris (Spigelian), incisions.
Inguinal canal: deep ring (transversalis fascia) → superficial ring (EO).
Contents: spermatic cord / round ligament, ilio-inguinal nerve.
Indirect hernia lateral, direct medial to inferior epigastric vessels.
Posterior wall: psoas, quadratus lumborum, iliacus, diaphragm.

high_yield.html: Rule of 3: skin, Camper's (fatty), Scarpa's (membranous) → external oblique, internal oblique, transversus → transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum.

Inguinal canal (~4 cm): deep ring in transversalis fascia (lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) → superficial ring in the external oblique aponeurosis (above the pubic tubercle). Contents: spermatic cord / round ligament + ilio-inguinal nerve.
Canal walls 'MALT' from above round: roof = Muscles (IO, TA arches); anterior = Aponeurosis of EO; floor = Ligament (inguinal); posterior = Transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon).

Indirect hernia: through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels (can reach the scrotum; common in young males). Direct: through the posterior wall, medial to them, in Hesselbach's triangle (older men).
Arcuate line: below it all aponeuroses pass in front of rectus; only transversalis fascia lies behind it.
Umbilical remnants: umbilical vein → ligamentum teres; urachus → median umbilical ligament; umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments.
Skin lymph: above the umbilicus → axillary nodes, below → superficial inguinal. Weak spots: umbilicus, linea semilunaris (Spigelian), incisions.
Iliopsoas on the posterior wall: an inflamed retrocaecal appendix or psoas abscess gives pain on hip extension (psoas sign).

deeper.title: Why indirect inguinal hernias are common in boys
deeper.html:
The testis descends through the inguinal canal before birth, dragging a pouch of peritoneum (the processus vaginalis) with it. If this pouch fails to close, it leaves an open path from the abdomen through the deep ring into the scrotum. Bowel can slip down that path, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels: an indirect hernia, the most common type, especially in male infants.

Source: the lecture's inguinal canal embryology and hernia slides.

exam_points: Bile: 600-1000 mL/day; bilirubin from haemoglobin; enterohepatic circulation via ileum.
Intrahepatic ducts follow segments; variants common.
Confluence at the hilum within the hilar plate; left duct long, right duct short.
Common hepatic + cystic → common bile duct.
CBD: hepatoduodenal ligament → retroduodenal → intrapancreatic → ampulla → D2.
Sphincter of Oddi at the major papilla.
Gallbladder under segments 4b-5: fundus, body, neck; valve of Heister.
Hepatocystic triangle + cystic artery; critical view of safety.
Cystic artery supplies the gallbladder.
Sympathetic: storage, pain; vagus: release; right phrenic: Glisson's capsule.

high_yield.html: Right + left hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct; + cystic duct → common bile duct → behind D1 → through the pancreatic head → joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater → major papilla (D2), controlled by the sphincter of Oddi.

Calot's (hepatocystic) triangle: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior border of the liver; contains the cystic artery (usually from the right hepatic). Obtain the critical view of safety before clipping.
Cholecystectomy danger: mistaking the common bile duct for the cystic duct, or the right hepatic artery for the cystic artery; biliary and arterial variants are common.
Biliary colic/cholecystitis: RUQ pain referred to the right shoulder (phrenic) and inferior angle of the scapula. A stone in the CBD → obstructive jaundice; at the ampulla → gallstone pancreatitis.
Gallbladder: fundus, body, neck; lies under segments 4b-5; the cystic duct has the spiral valve of Heister. The fundus projects at the tip of the 9th right costal cartilage (Murphy's sign).
Bile: 600-1000 mL/day; enterohepatic circulation: bile salts reabsorbed in the terminal ileum → portal vein → liver. CCK contracts the gallbladder; vagus promotes release.
Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier) suggests a tumour of the pancreatic head or ampulla rather than stones.

deeper.title: Why a gallstone can cause jaundice and pancreatitis
deeper.html:
The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct usually join at the hepatopancreatic ampulla before opening into the duodenum. A stone lodged there blocks bile, so bilirubin backs up into the blood (jaundice), and can also block or divert pancreatic juice, triggering acute pancreatitis. This shared exit explains why gallstones are a leading cause of both.

Source: the lecture's hepatopancreatic ampulla slide.

figure.caption: From the liver to the duodenum. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Gallbladder: fundus, body, neck → cystic duct

provenance.note: Colon anatomy (EFM lectures, 2025-26) (Anatomy 2, Pr. A. Majbar)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Colon: water absorption, vitamins K and B, faeces storage.
Unique features: taeniae coli, haustra, omental appendices.
Caecum: right iliac fossa (75%), intraperitoneal.
Appendix: 6-10 cm; base where taeniae converge; McBurney's point; variable tip.
Ascending (right flank) → hepatic flexure → transverse (mesocolon) → splenic flexure → descending → sigmoid.
Sigmoid: ~40 cm, mesocolon over left ureter.
SMA: ileocolic, right colic, middle colic.
IMA: left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal.
Marginal artery links SMA and IMA.
Lymph: epicolic → paracolic → intermediate → mesenteric nodes.

high_yield.html: Colon hallmarks: taeniae coli (3 bands), haustra, epiploic appendices. The small intestine has none of them.

Appendix base is where the three taeniae converge (surgical landmark). McBurney's point: one third of the way from the ASIS to the umbilicus. The tip position varies (retrocaecal most often), so pain location varies.
Appendicitis pain starts periumbilical (visceral, T10, midgut) then moves to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is irritated.
SMA (midgut): ileocolic, right colic, middle colic. IMA (hindgut): left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal. The marginal artery links them.
Watershed areas (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) sit between two arterial territories: most vulnerable in ischaemic colitis.
Intraperitoneal: caecum (mostly), transverse and sigmoid colon (mobile on a mesocolon). Retroperitoneal: ascending and descending colon.
The sigmoid mesocolon root lies over the left ureter: identify the ureter in sigmoid surgery. Sigmoid mobility → volvulus.
Lymph follows the arteries (epicolic → paracolic → intermediate → main), so cancer surgery removes the colon with its mesentery and vascular pedicle.

deeper.title: Why the splenic flexure is vulnerable to ischaemia
deeper.html:
The splenic flexure sits at the boundary between the SMA (midgut) and IMA (hindgut) territories. Only the marginal artery connects them there, and in some people this link is thin. When blood pressure drops or one artery is blocked, this watershed zone is the first to suffer, making ischaemic colitis most common at the splenic flexure.

Source: the lecture's arterial supply slides.

figure.caption: Midgut (SMA) up to two thirds of the transverse colon, hindgut (IMA) beyond. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Marginal artery links all branches along the colon

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Largest abdominal organ; ~2% of adult weight.
Double inflow (portal vein, hepatic artery), double outflow (hepatic veins, bile ducts).
Mostly right hypochondrium; upper border 5th right rib to 6th left rib.
Surfaces: diaphragmatic, visceral, posterior (bare area, IVC groove).
Ligaments: falciform, round (umbilical vein), coronary, triangular, lesser omentum, ligamentum venosum (ductus venosus).
Lobes: right, left, quadrate, caudate.
Hepatoduodenal ligament: portal triad; Pringle manoeuvre.
Portosystemic anastomoses: oesophageal, paraumbilical, rectal, retroperitoneal.
Couinaud: 2 hemilivers, 4 sectors, 8 segments; middle hepatic vein divides halves.
Segment 1 = caudate lobe.
Nerves: hepatic plexus; intercostals to Glisson's capsule.

high_yield.html: Double inflow (portal vein ~75%, hepatic artery ~25%) and double outflow (hepatic veins → IVC; bile ducts).
Ligament remnants: ligamentum teres = umbilical vein; ligamentum venosum = ductus venosus. The falciform ligament carries the teres in its free edge.
Caudate lobe (between IVC and ligamentum venosum) = segment 1, drains directly into the IVC. Quadrate lobe (between gallbladder and teres) is part of the functional left liver (segment 4).

Anatomical vs functional: anatomically the falciform ligament divides right and left lobes; functionally the dividing plane is the middle hepatic vein (Cantlie's line, gallbladder to IVC). Couinaud: 8 segments.

Bare area (between the coronary ligament layers) touches the diaphragm directly. Hepatorenal pouch (Morison's) is the lowest part of the upper abdominal cavity when lying supine: fluid collects there.
Portosystemic anastomoses: oesophageal (varices), paraumbilical (caput medusae), rectal (anorectal varices), retroperitoneal.

Pringle manoeuvre (clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament) stops portal and arterial inflow; bleeding that continues comes from the hepatic veins/IVC. Liver biopsy in the right mid-axillary line risks pneumothorax.
Glisson's capsule pain is carried by lower intercostal and phrenic fibres → right upper quadrant and right shoulder pain.

deeper.title: Why surgeons use segments, not lobes
deeper.html:
The four anatomical lobes are defined by surface features and do not match the internal blood supply: the quadrate lobe, for example, is fed by the left portal pedicle. Couinaud's eight segments each have their own portal, arterial and biliary pedicle and are separated by the hepatic veins, so a surgeon can remove one or more segments while leaving the rest fully supplied and drained.

Source: the lecture's functional division slides.

figure.caption: 8 segments, 4 sectors, 2 hemilivers. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Middle hepatic vein / main portal fissure (Cantlie)
Left HV / umbilical fissure: left sectors

title: Lymphatics and innervation of the abdomen
subject: subj:anat2

provenance.note: Lymphatics and innervation of the abdomen (Anatomy 2) (Anatomy 2, Pr. A. Souadka)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Lymph: fluid balance, immune surveillance, fat absorption.
Thoracic duct → left subclavian vein.
Parietal lymph follows veins; visceral lymph follows arteries.
Foregut → coeliac; midgut → SMA; hindgut → IMA nodes.
Cisterna chyli: L1-L2, 5-7 cm → thoracic duct at T12.
Oesophagus: longitudinal submucosal lymphatics; upper → cervical, middle → mediastinal, lower → coeliac.
Wall nerves: thoracoabdominal T7-T11, subcostal T12, iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal L1, genitofemoral L1-L2.
Greater splanchnic T5-T9 → coeliac; lesser T10-T11 → SM; least T12 → aorticorenal; lumbar L1-L2 → IM.
Vagus: to 2/3 transverse colon; pelvic splanchnics S2-S4: hindgut and pelvis.
ENS: myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses.

high_yield.html: Visceral lymph follows the arteries (foregut → coeliac, midgut → SMA, hindgut → IMA nodes); parietal lymph follows the veins.
Cisterna chyli at L1-L2 → thoracic duct (through the aortic hiatus, T12) → left subclavian/internal jugular junction.
Lymphatic injury in surgery → chylous ascites (milky fluid). Gastric cancer can spread up the thoracic duct to the left supraclavicular node (Virchow's, Troisier's sign).
Splanchnic nerves: greater (T5-T9) → coeliac; lesser (T10-T11) → superior mesenteric; least (T12) → aorticorenal; lumbar (L1-L2) → inferior mesenteric.
Parasympathetic: vagus as far as the distal third of the transverse colon (midgut/hindgut boundary); beyond it pelvic splanchnics S2-S4.
Referred visceral pain follows the sympathetic level: foregut → epigastrium, midgut → umbilicus, hindgut → suprapubic region.
Wall nerves: T7-T11 thoracoabdominal, T12 subcostal, L1 iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal (the latter through the inguinal canal), L1-L2 genitofemoral (cremaster: genital branch).
Cremasteric reflex (stroke the inner thigh → testis rises): afferent femoral branch, efferent genital branch of genitofemoral (L1-L2).

deeper.title: Why appendicitis pain starts around the umbilicus
deeper.html:
Visceral pain travels with sympathetic fibres back to the spinal segments that supplied the embryonic gut. The appendix is a midgut organ, so early inflamed-appendix pain is felt vaguely around the umbilicus (T10). Only when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic nerves, does the pain move to a precise spot in the right iliac fossa.

Source: the lecture's somatic and visceral innervation slides.

figure.caption: Sympathetic splanchnics vs parasympathetic vagus and pelvic splanchnics. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Lesser T10-T11 → SM ganglion; least T12 → aorticorenal
Lumbar splanchnics L1-L2 → IM ganglion, hypogastric
Vagus (CN X): foregut + midgut (to 2/3 transverse colon)
Pelvic splanchnics S2-S4: hindgut, bladder, genitals

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Pancreas: 12-20 cm, retroperitoneal, in front of L1-L2.
Exocrine (acini) + endocrine (islets: insulin, glucagon).
Parts: head, uncinate process, neck, body, tail.
Head in the duodenal C; CBD in a posterior groove; on IVC.
Uncinate process behind SMA/SMV.
Neck over the portal vein (SMV + splenic vein).
Body over aorta and L2; tail in splenorenal ligament to splenic hilum.
Wirsung + CBD → ampulla of Vater → major papilla; Santorini → minor papilla.
Variants: annular pancreas, pancreas divisum.
Head: superior (GDA) + inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arcades; body/tail: splenic artery.
Veins: head → SMV/portal; body/tail → splenic vein.

high_yield.html: Retroperitoneal, L1-L2. Parts: head (in the duodenal C), uncinate process (behind SMA/SMV), neck (in front of the portal vein), body (over aorta, L2), tail (in the splenorenal ligament, reaching the splenic hilum; the only intraperitoneal part).
Portal vein forms behind the neck from the SMV + splenic vein.
Ducts: main (Wirsung) + CBD → ampulla of Vater → major papilla; accessory (Santorini) → minor papilla.
Annular pancreas (ventral bud ring around D2) → duodenal obstruction; pancreas divisum (buds' ducts don't fuse) → most juice drains through the minor papilla: the commonest variant.

Double supply: head from superior (GDA, coeliac) and inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arcades; body and tail from the splenic artery. That is why the head and duodenum are removed together (Whipple).
Head tumour compresses the CBD → painless obstructive jaundice; body/tail tumour → back pain, late presentation. Pancreatic pain radiates to the back.
Splenic vein runs behind the pancreas: pancreatitis or tumour → splenic vein thrombosis → isolated gastric varices.

deeper.title: Why pancreatic head cancer causes painless jaundice
deeper.html:
The common bile duct runs in a groove on the back of the pancreatic head and then through it to the ampulla. A tumour growing in the head squeezes the duct long before it causes much pain, so bile backs up: the patient turns yellow, with dark urine and pale stools, and a palpable, distended gallbladder may be felt. Tumours of the body and tail lack this early warning and are usually found later.

Source: the lecture's head relations and duct slides.

figure.alt: Parts of the pancreas and their relations
figure.caption: Head to tail, across the spine at L1-L2. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Head: in the duodenal C, CBD behind, on IVC
Neck: over the portal vein (SMV + splenic)
Body: over aorta and L2, floor of lesser sac
Wirsung → major papilla; Santorini → minor papilla

title: Pelvic vessels, lymphatics and autonomic nerves
subject: subj:anat2

provenance.note: Pelvic vessels, lymphatics and autonomic nervous system (2025-26) (Anatomy 2, Pr. O. Lahnaoui)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Aorta bifurcates at L4; common iliac divides at L5/S1.
External iliac → femoral; internal iliac → pelvis and perineum.
Internal iliac: ~4 cm; anterior (visceral) and posterior (parietal) divisions.
Anterior: superior vesical, inferior vesical/vaginal, uterine, middle rectal, obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal.
Posterior: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal.
Uterine artery crosses over the ureter ('water under the bridge').
Internal pudendal: out via greater, back via lesser sciatic foramen.
Rectal venous plexus: superior → portal; middle/inferior → systemic.
Nodes: external iliac, internal iliac, obturator, presacral → common iliac.
Sympathetic T10-L2 → superior hypogastric → inferior hypogastric: storage, ejaculation.
Parasympathetic S2-S4 (nervi erigentes): micturition, defecation, erection.
S2-S4 lesion → flaccid bladder; above S2 → spastic bladder.

high_yield.html: Aorta bifurcates at L4; common iliac divides at the sacroiliac joint (L5/S1) into external iliac (→ femoral) and internal iliac (pelvis, perineum, gluteal region).
'Water under the bridge': the ureter (water) passes under the uterine artery (bridge) near the cervix; the main site of ureteric injury in hysterectomy.
Internal iliac: posterior division = iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal (parietal only). Anterior = vesicals, uterine/vaginal, middle rectal, obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal.

Internal pudendal artery leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks round the ischial spine and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen (the pudendal nerve takes the same route).

Rectal veins: superior → IMV → portal; middle and inferior → internal iliac → systemic: a portosystemic anastomosis. Left common iliac vein is compressed by the right common iliac artery → left-sided DVT (May-Thurner).
Sympathetic (T10-L2) via the hypogastric plexuses = storage and ejaculation. Parasympathetic S2-S4 (nervi erigentes) = voiding, defecation, erection ('point and shoot').

Lesion above S2 → spastic (reflex) bladder; lesion of S2-S4/cauda equina → flaccid bladder with overflow incontinence. Rectal or pelvic surgery can damage the plexuses → retention and erectile dysfunction.
Nodes: obturator (prostate, cervix staging), internal and external iliac, presacral → common iliac → para-aortic.

deeper.title: Why hysterectomy can injure the ureter
deeper.html:
Near the cervix, the uterine artery passes over the ureter just before reaching the uterus, about 2 cm lateral to the cervix. When surgeons clamp the uterine vessels, the ureter lies directly beneath; a clamp placed too low or too lateral can crush or tie it. The memory aid 'water under the bridge' (ureter under artery) reminds surgeons to identify it first.

Source: the lecture's uterine artery slide.

provenance.note: Perineum and pelvic floor anatomy (EFM lectures) (Anatomy 2, Pr. A. Majbar)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Pelvic floor: levator ani + coccygeus; separates pelvis from perineum.
Functions: organ support, continence, sexual function.
Perineum: urogenital (anterior) and anal (posterior) triangles, divided at the ischial tuberosities.
Superficial perineal space: ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal.
Deep perineal space: external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal.
Anal triangle: anal canal, external anal sphincter, ischioanal fossae.
Perineal body: central attachment point.
Levator ani: puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus.
Puborectalis sling: anorectal angle, faecal continence.
Weakness → prolapse and incontinence.

high_yield.html: Pelvic diaphragm = levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) + coccygeus; supplied by S3-S4 and the pudendal nerve.
Perineum (diamond): a line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the anterior urogenital and posterior anal triangles.

Superficial perineal space: ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal + erectile tissue + greater vestibular glands. Deep space: external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal, bulbourethral glands (male).
Puborectalis sling maintains the anorectal angle: key for faecal continence.
The perineal body is the central anchor of the perineal muscles; tearing it in childbirth (or an episiotomy that extends) weakens support → prolapse and incontinence.
Ischioanal fossae (fat-filled, either side of the anal canal) can harbour abscesses that spread around the back (horseshoe abscess).
Internal anal sphincter = smooth, involuntary (autonomic); external anal sphincter = skeletal, voluntary (pudendal nerve, inferior rectal branch).

deeper.title: Why childbirth can lead to prolapse years later
deeper.html:
During vaginal delivery the baby's head stretches the levator ani and the perineal body, and can tear them or injure the pudendal nerve. The damage may be silent at first, but with ageing and loss of oestrogen the weakened floor no longer supports the bladder, uterus and rectum against abdominal pressure, so they sag into the vagina. Pelvic floor exercises and repair of perineal tears aim to prevent this.

Source: the lecture's clinical applications on prolapse and incontinence.

figure.caption: The pelvic diaphragm above, the perineal triangles below. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Pelvic diaphragm: levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) + coccygeus
Urogenital triangle: superficial space (ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse) + deep space
Anal triangle: anal canal, external anal sphincter, ischioanal fossae

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Small intestine: 6-7 m, pylorus → ileocaecal junction; digestion, absorption, motility.
Duodenum 20-30 cm, jejunum ~2.5 m (2/5), ileum ~3.5 m (3/5).
Plicae, villi, microvilli increase surface.
Cells: enterocytes, goblet, Paneth, enteroendocrine.
Duodenum: C-shaped, mostly retroperitoneal, 4 parts.
Major papilla in D2; SMA crosses D3; ligament of Treitz at D4.
Duodenum supply: coeliac + SMA (pancreaticoduodenal).
Brunner's glands (duodenum); Peyer's patches (ileum).
Jejunum/ileum intraperitoneal on a mesentery.
SMA gives 15-18 branches → arcades → vasa recta.

high_yield.html: Duodenum: 4 parts; only D1 (cap) is intraperitoneal, the rest retroperitoneal. D2 = major papilla (bile + pancreatic ducts); D3 crossed by the SMA/SMV; D4 → duodenojejunal flexure (ligament of Treitz).
The major papilla marks the foregut/midgut junction: above it supply is coeliac (superior pancreaticoduodenal via GDA), below it SMA (inferior pancreaticoduodenal).
Jejunum vs ileum: jejunum = wider, thicker, redder, tall plicae, long vasa recta, few arcades; ileum = narrower, Peyer's patches, short vasa recta, many arcades, more mesenteric fat.
Glands: Brunner's (submucosa of the duodenum, alkaline mucus); Paneth cells (crypts, antimicrobial); Peyer's patches (ileum). Lengths: duodenum 25 cm, jejunum 2/5, ileum 3/5 of the rest.
The ligament of Treitz divides upper from lower GI bleeding. The terminal ileum absorbs B12 and bile salts: resection or Crohn's disease there → B12 deficiency and fat malabsorption.
SMA syndrome: D3 squeezed between the SMA and aorta (after rapid weight loss) → proximal obstruction. Mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion to the findings.

deeper.title: Why the SMA can squeeze the duodenum
deeper.html:
The third part of the duodenum crosses the spine in the angle between the aorta behind and the superior mesenteric artery in front. Normally a fat pad keeps this angle open. After major weight loss the angle narrows and the artery can compress the duodenum (superior mesenteric artery syndrome), causing vomiting after meals. The same relationship explains why the D3 region matters in trauma and surgery.

Source: the lecture's duodenum description.

figure.caption: Distinguishing features. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Jejunum (2/5, ~2.5 m): wide, thick, red; long vasa recta, 1-2 arcades
Ileum (3/5, ~3.5 m): narrower, short vasa recta, many arcades
Peyer's patches; ends at ileocaecal junction

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Spleen: 10-12 cm, 150-200 g; intraperitoneal except hilum.
Largest lymphoid mass: immune surveillance.
Left hypochondrium, against ribs 9-11, long axis along rib 10.
Normally not palpable below the costal margin.
Surfaces: diaphragmatic and visceral; hilum.
7 ligaments: gastrosplenic (short gastrics), splenorenal (splenic vessels + pancreatic tail), splenophrenic, splenocolic, phrenicocolic, pancreaticosplenic, pancreaticocolic.
Splenic artery: largest coeliac branch, along upper pancreas.
Segmental branching allows partial splenectomy.
Splenic vein behind pancreas + SMV → portal vein.
Lymph to coeliac/SMA nodes; nerves from vagus and splanchnics.

high_yield.html: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11: about 1 × 3 × 5 inches, ~7 oz (150-200 g), lies under ribs 9 to 11 (long axis along rib 10).
Intraperitoneal (except the hilum), in the left hypochondrium; not normally palpable. When enlarged it grows down and towards the right iliac fossa, with a palpable notch on its anterior border.
Gastrosplenic ligament = short gastric + left gastroepiploic vessels; splenorenal ligament = splenic vessels + tail of the pancreas.
Left lower rib fractures can rupture the spleen → haemorrhage and Kehr's sign (left shoulder pain via the phrenic nerve). The pancreatic tail is at risk during splenectomy.
Splenic artery = largest coeliac branch, tortuous, along the upper border of the pancreas; divides into segmental branches (partial splenectomy possible). Splenic vein + SMV → portal vein.
After splenectomy: lifelong risk of overwhelming infection by encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae b, meningococcus): vaccinate.

deeper.title: Why people without a spleen need vaccines
deeper.html:
The spleen filters blood and its lymphoid tissue makes antibodies and clears bacteria coated with them, especially encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus. After splenectomy, these infections can become overwhelming within hours. That is why patients are vaccinated against these bacteria and told to seek care urgently for any fever.

Source: the lecture's splenic functions and splenectomy slides.

figure.caption: Peritoneal folds linking it to neighbours. Schematic drawn for this site.

exam_points: Oesophagus: 25 cm, C6 → T11; hiatus T10.
UES and LES; GERD, achalasia.
Epithelium: non-keratinised stratified squamous; no serosa (adventitia).
Muscle: upper 1/3 skeletal, middle mixed, lower 1/3 smooth.
Thoracic oesophagus: left atrium in front, aorta on the left.
Left gastric vein → portal: portosystemic anastomosis (varices).
Stomach: cardia, fundus, body, pylorus; intraperitoneal.
Lesser omentum: hepatogastric + hepatoduodenal (portal triad); Winslow foramen; Pringle.
Greater omentum: gastrocolic, gastrosplenic, gastrophrenic.
Lesser curvature: L + R gastric; greater: L + R gastroepiploic; fundus: short gastrics.
Vagus stimulates; coeliac plexus inhibits.
Peptic ulcer: H. pylori, NSAIDs.

high_yield.html: Oesophagus: 25 cm, C6 → T11, through the diaphragm at T10. Muscle: upper 1/3 skeletal, middle mixed, lower 1/3 smooth. No serosa (adventitia).
Oesophageal constrictions at about 15, 25 and 40 cm from the incisors: cricopharyngeus, aortic arch/left main bronchus, diaphragm. Swallowed objects lodge there.
Left gastric vein ↔ oesophageal (azygos) veins = portosystemic anastomosis: in portal hypertension → oesophageal varices, a cause of massive haematemesis.

Gastric arteries (all from the coeliac trunk): lesser curvature = left gastric (coeliac) + right gastric (hepatic); greater curvature = left gastroepiploic (splenic) + right gastroepiploic (gastroduodenal); fundus = short gastrics (splenic).
Lesser omentum = hepatogastric + hepatoduodenal ligaments; the latter carries the portal triad and forms the front of the epiploic foramen (Winslow) into the lesser sac.
Posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery → major bleed; posterior gastric ulcer → splenic artery or pancreas. Pringle manoeuvre = clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament.
Vagus stimulates acid and motility; sympathetic (coeliac plexus) inhibits. Stomach is intraperitoneal; the lesser sac lies behind it, in front of the pancreas.
GERD = LES failure; achalasia = LES fails to relax (loss of myenteric neurons).

deeper.title: Why cirrhosis causes oesophageal varices
deeper.html:
The lower oesophagus drains both into the left gastric vein (portal system) and into the azygos veins (systemic). When liver scarring blocks portal flow, portal blood seeks detours through this junction; the thin submucosal veins of the lower oesophagus swell into varices, which can rupture and bleed massively. The same anatomy explains why this is a classic portosystemic anastomosis.

Source: the lecture's venous drainage slide.

exam_points: Abdominal aorta: T12 → bifurcation at L4.
Coeliac trunk (T12): left gastric, common hepatic, splenic; foregut.
SMA (L1): midgut; ileocolic, right and middle colic.
IMA (L3): hindgut; left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal.
Renal arteries L1-L2; gonadal arteries below them.
Posterior: inferior phrenic, lumbar arteries.
IVC: common iliacs at L5 → diaphragm at T8; right of aorta.
IVC tributaries: none from gut or spleen; left gonadal → left renal vein.
Portal vein: SMV + splenic (+ IMV) + gastric veins.
Portosystemic: oesophageal, paraumbilical, rectal, retroperitoneal; TIPS.

high_yield.html: Abdominal aorta: enters at T12, bifurcates at L4 (umbilicus level). Gut arteries: coeliac T12 (foregut), SMA L1 (midgut), IMA L3 (hindgut). Renals ~L1-L2.

Coeliac trunk = left gastric, common hepatic (→ GDA, proper hepatic, right gastric), splenic. SMA = inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal/ileal, ileocolic, right and middle colic. IMA = left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal.
IVC: forms at L5, right of the aorta, pierces the central tendon at T8. It receives no gut or spleen blood (that goes via the portal vein).
Left gonadal vein → left renal vein; right gonadal → IVC directly. So a left renal tumour or vein obstruction can cause a left varicocele.
Nutcracker: the left renal vein runs between the SMA and aorta and can be compressed there.
Portal vein = SMV + splenic vein (IMV usually joins the splenic). Portosystemic sites: oesophageal, paraumbilical, rectal, retroperitoneal. TIPS decompresses portal hypertension.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm: usually infrarenal; pulsatile mass above the umbilicus; repaired open or by stent graft.

deeper.title: Why a left varicocele can signal a kidney tumour
deeper.html:
The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle, while the right testicular vein enters the IVC directly. A left renal tumour extending into the renal vein can block that outflow, so the left pampiniform plexus swells into a varicocele. A new left varicocele in an adult, especially one that does not empty when lying down, prompts imaging of the left kidney.

Source: the lecture's gonadal vessels and IVC tributaries.
